title: Lamplighter streets
kernel: A state is both the walker's integer position and the finite set of lamps that are on. One move is left one, right one, or toggle the lamp at the current position. Starting all off at position 0, reaching lamps {-1,0,1} on with walker back at 0 takes 7 moves: 3 toggles and at least 4 walks. From that target, each of its three neighboring states has distance 6 from the start. Thus every legal next move can move closer to the original start. Do not confuse distance to the target with distance from the all-off start. For a target lamp set and final position, the fewest moves equal required toggles plus a shortest line walk visiting those lamps and ending at the required position. This is a concrete lamplighter-group word metric, not Week 2's edge-toggle invariant.
sources: https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~kapovich/EPR/ggt.pdf (Exercise 7.82, printed p. 233; PDF p. 253); https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0309344 (dead-end examples, PDF p. 9).
materials: A numbered line mat, one clearly different walker pawn, and two-sided lamp counters large enough to flip. Per pair: 9 counters for positions -4 through 4, one pawn, pencil. A partner checks that only the lamp under the pawn can flip and preserves the pawn in the final-state diagram. Record one move word if needed, not simultaneous tallies.

title: Meeting on shortest roads
kernel: For three vertices of a rectangular unit grid with Manhattan distance, the unique vertex belonging to some shortest route for each pair is (median x, median y). For homes (0,0), (4,1), (1,4), it is (1,1). It need not lie on every chosen shortest path, and is not merely the location minimizing total distance. A tree has an analogous unique three-way meeting vertex. The graph that is just a 3-cycle has no vertex on shortest paths for all three pairs. On a cube, the common vertex is coordinatewise majority: 000,110,101 give 100. These are median graphs and intervals. Keep the three pairwise conditions simultaneous on one unchanged board.
materials: Per pair: three home counters and one meeting counter, three colored pencils, square-grid board and tree/cycle drawings. Roads are horizontal or vertical grid edges, never diagonals. Optional cube uses a paper net or eight connected vertex dots with three binary labels; no specialist blocks required.

title: How many ways out
kernel: Ends describe components continuing infinitely far after deleting a finite region, as larger finite deletions are considered. A two-way infinite line and an infinite ladder have two ends. The infinite square grid has one end: any finite blocked region fits inside a box, and sufficiently far-out points can connect around that box. An infinite 3-regular tree has infinitely many ends; removing a center vertex gives 3 infinite components, then centered balls of radius 1 and 2 give 6 and 12 components. A finite drawing is only a window with explicit continuation; boundary exits on a finite board are not themselves a proof of ends. Distinguish a finite isolated pocket from a component continuing forever.
materials: Per pair: a printed road window, blackout counters or opaque paper squares, pencils in several colors. Arrows at every continuation edge identify the intended infinite pattern. Cover vertices and incident roads, never ambiguously cover just a drawn region. Use finite windows to test conjectures and enlarging-window reasoning to discuss forever.

title: Thin and fat road triangles
kernel: A geodesic triangle chooses one shortest path between each pair of three vertices. Every tree triangle is a tripod: each chosen side lies in the union of the other two, so it is 0-thin. In the integer square grid, take A=(0,0), B=(n,0), C=(n,n), AB along the bottom and BC along the right, and AC along the left then top. The corner (0,n) on AC is distance n from the other two sides, measured using any roads in the full grid, not only the triangle boundary. This family prevents a uniform thinness bound for the infinite grid. Finite experiments are not a proof about all triangles or all scales. Do not claim grid triangles must all be fat.
materials: Per pair: 3 colored pencils or strings, home counters, ruler for counting grid edges, tree and square-grid boards. Shortest distance to a side means the fewest road edges to any point of that side; roads in the interior remain usable. Child controls where the triangle sides go, subject to being shortest.

title: Four shields in a portal room
kernel: In a square flat torus with side length 4, source S=(0,0) and target T=(2,2), every straight trajectory from S to T has a lift ending at (2+4m,2+4n). Its midpoint (1+2m,1+2n), reduced modulo 4, is one of (1,1),(1,3),(3,1),(3,3); therefore four point shields block every trajectory. Four are necessary because the four diagonal half-period paths from S to T have disjoint interiors and require separate shields. Shields cannot occupy source or target. Intermediate visits to the target count as an earlier hit. Distinguish continuous straight travel and wraparound from graph walks. This is finite blocking, not merely the torus lift apparatus in Week 41.
sources: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.2975 (Lemma 12, PDF p. 12, torus midpoint blocking).
materials: Per pair: portal square with opposite edges explicitly paired, four small point counters, pencil and straightedge, plus a tiled unfolded square window for tracing. Use points, not discs with a positive blocking radius. Duplicate seam labels represent one location. Show a simple seam crossing before asking children to use an unfolded map.

title: Can you hear the room
kernel: A bounce word records the successive side labels struck by a non-corner billiard trajectory in a labeled polygon. For two adjacent sides A and B, the finite word ABA is impossible in a rectangle but possible at an acute 60-degree corner of a 60-degree rhombus. Exclude corner hits. A witnessed word can eliminate a candidate only when impossible there; failure to find one by trial is not proof. All labeled rectangles, whatever their aspect ratio, have the same full bounce-word language by coordinate scaling and unfolding, despite lengths/angles of individual trajectories changing. A finite observation cannot generally determine the room. The activity should involve choosing and physically checking candidate rays, not memorizing a catalog of hidden answers.
sources: https://justinlanier.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/bounce.pdf (introductory examples, pp. 3–6); https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.05690 (bounce spectra and rigidity).
materials: Per pair: labeled candidate room drawings (square, nonsquare rectangle, 60-degree rhombus), ruler, pencil, and small mirror or reflected paper copies where useful. Build exact reflected candidate rays using a provided tracing window rather than require children to aim a real ball precisely. Provide explicit input/intermediate/output example for a bounce word, using a non-task word.

title: A robot that remembers area
kernel: The robot state is integer position (x,y) and counter z. E/W change x by +/-1; N changes y by +1 and adds the current x to z; S changes y by -1 and subtracts the current x. Beginning (0,0,0), the six monotone two-E/two-N paths to (2,2) give EENN:4, ENEN:3, ENNE:2, NEEN:2, NENE:1, NNEE:0. E,N,W,S is a closed unit loop with counter +1; reversal changes the sign. Thus position does not determine the state, and loops leave signed area memory. The group law (x,y,z)(a,b,c)=(x+a,y+b,z+c+xb) is an integer Heisenberg model. This is distinct from merely maximizing area: the new destination is noncommuting motion and extra central memory. Avoid conflating the integral convention with symmetric height conventions differing by xy/2.
sources: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.5276 (Heisenberg geometry and signed area, PDF p. 3).
materials: Per pair: integer-grid mat, robot counter, movable number line or counter tray for memory, E/W/N/S cards and pencil. Printed columns carry their values to externalize the addition rule. A partner operates the counter and checks the robot, rotating roles. Demonstrate a non-task path with position and memory shown at meaningful intermediate steps.

title: The gentlest stretch
kernel: Compare a side-marked 4-by-1 rectangle and a 2-by-2 square with Euclidean distances. Among homeomorphisms carrying each named side to its corresponding side, the smallest possible worst pairwise distance ratio is 2. Lower bound: a unit vertical segment in the rectangle joins opposite horizontal boundaries, whose images are at least 2 apart in the square. Upper bound: (x,y)->(x/2,2y) stretches every pair by at most 2 and preserves the required sides. Sparse pin measurements give only lower bounds; a proposed map needs a rule for the whole sheet. This is a Lipschitz comparison, not the Teichmuller metric. A child-controlled model should let children choose and test correspondences or stretch designs; avoid making this an adult lecture with decorative rubber bands.
sources: Metric comparison inspired by https://people.reed.edu/~davidp/talks/talks05-06/talks/duchin.html (Moon Duchin, November 3, 2005, Billiards and Geometric Topology). The elementary side-preserving Lipschitz calculation is developed here; no claim it occurred in the talk.
materials: Per pair: side-marked rectangle/square drawings to scale, movable labeled paper dots, ruler, thread lengths or paper strips for distance comparison, and blank grids for children’s alternative maps. Do not rely on stretching real rubber uniformly. Provide a workable paper-based mapping game with clear legal conditions; adult notes must honestly distinguish finite samples from a whole continuous map.

title: Doubling elevators
kernel: At nonnegative level h, a horizontal left/right move changes ground coordinate x by 2^h and costs one; up/down changes h by one and leaves x fixed. Start (0,0), finish (16,0). Eight moves suffice: up twice, right four times, down twice. Any route of at most seven moves reaching maximum height H uses at least 2H vertical moves, hence has displacement at most (7-2H)2^H. For H=0,1,2,3 the bounds are 7,10,12,8, all below 16. This is a concrete exponential shortcut/subgroup-distortion model related to BS(1,2), not the full Cayley graph. Restricting a finite board or drawing only nonnegative levels must not be misrepresented as the whole group. Routes may go left or change levels more than once.
materials: Per pair: elevator road board with clearly marked level and ground coordinate, pawn, move cards or a single recorded move word. All levels align to the same horizontal coordinate scale; an up arrow never silently changes x. If high-level ticks skip labels, vertical connections still must land at the same x. Use a enough-width working strip; no physical specialist apparatus.

title: Twists on a cylinder
kernel: An annulus is a cylinder with two boundary circles. A Dehn twist fixes both boundary circles pointwise but adds one winding to a strand joining corresponding fixed endpoints. In angular/height coordinates, (theta,t)->(theta+2*pi*t,t) is such a map: at t=0 and t=1 the boundary points are unchanged modulo 2*pi. Composing twists adds winding; inverse twists cancel. Relative winding is visible after cutting the cylinder open and lifting to repeated rectangles. For two simple joining arcs with identical endpoints and winding numbers a,b, the minimum number of interior intersections is max(|a-b|-1,0), when shared endpoints are excluded; different endpoints change this formula, so do not guess from a picture. Keep endpoint/rim markings fixed, distinguish strand relaying from twisting a whole surface, and do not use a fake paper demonstration where simply rotating a ring undoes the intended effect.
sources: https://dianadavis.github.io/billiards-book.pdf (printed p. 111, Problem 111; PDF p. 129: torus shear and reassembly). This provides twisting/unfolding lineage. The fixed-boundary annulus model and interior-intersection formula are independently derived extensions, not claims attributed to that exercise.
materials: Per pair: ordinary paper cylinder with marked rims and seam, yarn or narrow removable paper strips, tape, and cut-open/repeated rectangle template. Use a workable strand-routing model with fixed taped endpoints and winding counted via seam crossings, or another physically accurate model. A rigid paper cylinder cannot literally undergo a smooth twist without deformation: describe the model honestly. Do not require untested specialized hinged sleeves. Physical rehearsal will remain explicitly untested.
